newsitem.title: UK: Oil trading patterns shift in high-price market.
newsitem.headline: Oil trading patterns shift in high-price market.

text.p: A drive by oil importing countries to diversify crude oil sources has been prompted partly by environmental concerns and partly by economics in a move away from traditional sales patterns, analysts and oil traders say.
"The real shift in crude supplies is occurring because of the large amounts of new available oil in the Atlantic Basin," said Peter Bogin of Cambridge Energy Research Associates.
"A lot of oil that was heading from the Middle East to Europe or the United States is being replaced by North Sea or Latin American oil, just because of geographic proximity," he added.
Saudi Arabia, the world's biggest oil producer and exporter, has not been affected much by the change and the United States continues to rely on the Gulf oil giant for secure supplies.

Nevertheless, Saudi supplies to the United States dropped to an average 4.6 million barrels per day (bpd) in 1995 from a Gulf War peak of 6.22 million bpd, U.S. Energy Information Administration (EIA) figures showed.

Oil traders say the United States is taking more oil from South American producers, who supply short-haul crude to refineries increasingly reluctant to sit on high crude stocks in a backwardated market where forward prices are below prompt ones.
"America used to rely more on long-haul crudes. There used to be a greater dependence on Saudi Arabia and other Gulf Arab producers," said the head of trading for a European oil company.

"The more recent game is to rely more on short-haul crude from Colombia, Venezuela, Mexico and it was coincidental that there was success in production in these areas and it makes sense to rely on the most proximate sources," the trader added.
Refineries adopted a cost-cutting policy of "just in time" buying in the belief that supply would outstrip demand once Iraqi crude began to flow and North Sea supplies peaked.

But Iraqi oil is still off the market, new production capacity in the North Sea has been delayed and OPEC countries did not take advantage of prices at near six-year highs to raise output beyond their self-imposed ceiling of 25.03 million bpd.
"The fact that short-haul crude is available has allowed refiners to rely much more on "just in time'," Bogin said. "If the U.S. had to rely on the Middle East, they couldn't do it."
The shift is not politically inspired although the United States has an embargo on imports from Iran and Libya.

Other countries like South Africa, which relied heavily on Iran for oil supplies during apartheid, has increased its purchases from Kuwait and is looking for other suppliers. Energy Minister Penuell Maduna said "it was not appropriate for a country to be so heavily reliant on one supplier.

A European trader said it was more the quality of crude needed to meet tougher environmental standards that determined purchasing patterns in the United States and Europe, where laws require lower sulphur emissions. This makes mostly light or sweet crudes like those produced in the North Sea the preferred grades.
Most Middle Eastern producers sell heavier, sour crude to the Far East, home to the world's fastest-growing economies where refineries are used to a diet of sour crudes.

Recently, the lifting of a U.S. ban on oil exports has meant Alaska North Slope (ANS), the U.S. sour benchmark, is being sold into Asia. South Korea took large amounts of the crude shunned by U.S. Gulf Coast refiners.

Analysts said there was even talk of reversing the oil pipeline running parallel to the Panama Canal because demand for ANS, which flows south from Alaska and eastwards into the U.S. Gulf coast, was too low in the main U.S. refining hub.
The other beneficiaries of rising demand for low sulphur, sweet crude have been West African producers and particularly Nigeria, whose crude prices have skyrocketed in recent weeks.

This month India, Taiwan and South Korea took an average 330,000 barrels of Nigerian crude daily despite the sharply higher cost of Nigerian grades against sour benchmark Dubai, which traditionally sells East of Suez.

A trader of West African crude oil said the daily average was below normal because Europe, where a lower sulphur specification came into effect this month, took more than an average amount of spot Nigerian October barrels.
Some Far Eastern countries are also bringing in tighter environmental laws and will be seeking lighter grades.
"The Asian market is growing faster than anywhere else as is their appetite for lighter sweet crudes," Bogin said.

The analysts say any change in trading patterns is unlikely to be sustained given the world's spare capacity lies mainly in the Middle East Gulf. North Sea production is expected to decline after peaking sometime before the end of the century.
